verses.text: Joab was told, “Behold, the king weeps and mourns for Absalom.”
The victory that day was turned into mourning among all the people; for the people heard it said that day, “The king grieves for his son.”
The people sneaked into the city that day, as people who are ashamed steal away when they flee in battle.
The king covered his face, and the king cried with a loud voice, “My son Absalom, Absalom, my son, my son!”

Joab came into the house to the king, and said, “Today you have shamed the faces of all your servants, who today have saved your life, and the lives of your sons and of your daughters, and the lives of your wives, and the lives of your concubines;

in that you love those who hate you, and hate those who love you. For you have declared today, that princes and servants are nothing to you. For today I perceive that if Absalom had lived, and all we had died today, then it would have pleased you well.

Now therefore arise, go out, and speak to comfort your servants; for I swear by Yahweh, if you don’t go out, not a man will stay with you this night. That would be worse to you than all the evil that has happened to you from your youth until now.”

Then the king arose, and sat in the gate. They told to all the people, saying, “Behold, the king is sitting in the gate.” All the people came before the king. Now Israel had fled every man to his tent.

All the people were at strife throughout all the tribes of Israel, saying, “The king delivered us out of the hand of our enemies, and he saved us out of the hand of the Philistines; and now he has fled out of the land from Absalom.
Absalom, whom we anointed over us, is dead in battle. Now therefore why don’t you speak a word of bringing the king back?”

King David sent to Zadok and to Abiathar the priests, saying, “Speak to the elders of Judah, saying, ‘Why are you the last to bring the king back to his house? Since the speech of all Israel has come to the king, to return him to his house.
You are my brothers. You are my bone and my flesh. Why then are you the last to bring back the king?’
Say to Amasa, ‘Aren’t you my bone and my flesh? God do so to me, and more also, if you aren’t captain of the army before me continually instead of Joab.’”
He bowed the heart of all the men of Judah, even as one man; so that they sent to the king, saying, “Return, you and all your servants.”
So the king returned, and came to the Jordan. Judah came to Gilgal, to go to meet the king, to bring the king over the Jordan.
Shimei the son of Gera, the Benjamite, who was of Bahurim, hurried and came down with the men of Judah to meet king David.

There were a thousand men of Benjamin with him, and Ziba the servant of Saul’s house, and his fifteen sons and his twenty servants with him; and they went through the Jordan in the presence of the king.
A ferry boat went to bring over the king’s household, and to do what he thought good. Shimei the son of Gera fell down before the king, when he had come over the Jordan.

He said to the king, “Don’t let my lord impute iniquity to me, or remember that which your servant did perversely the day that my lord the king went out of Jerusalem, that the king should take it to his heart.
For your servant knows that I have sinned. Therefore behold, I have come today as the first of all the house of Joseph to go down to meet my lord the king.”
But Abishai the son of Zeruiah answered, “Shouldn’t Shimei be put to death for this, because he cursed Yahweh’s anointed?”

David said, “What have I to do with you, you sons of Zeruiah, that you should be adversaries to me today? Shall any man be put to death today in Israel? For don’t I know that I am king over Israel today?”
The king said to Shimei, “You will not die.” The king swore to him.

Mephibosheth the son of Saul came down to meet the king; and he had neither groomed his feet, nor trimmed his beard, nor washed his clothes, from the day the king departed until the day he came home in peace.
When he had come to Jerusalem to meet the king, the king said to him, “Why didn’t you go with me, Mephibosheth?”
He answered, “My lord, O king, my servant deceived me. For your servant said, I will saddle me a donkey, that I may ride on it, and go with the king; because your servant is lame.
He has slandered your servant to my lord the king, but my lord the king is as an angel of God. Do therefore what is good in your eyes.

For all my father’s house were but dead men before my lord the king; yet you set your servant among those who ate at your own table. What right therefore have I yet that I should cry any more to the king?”
The king said to him, “Why do you speak any more of your matters? I say, you and Ziba divide the land.”
Mephibosheth said to the king, “Yes, let him take all, because my lord the king has come in peace to his own house.”
Barzillai the Gileadite came down from Rogelim; and he went over the Jordan with the king, to conduct him over the Jordan.
Now Barzillai was a very aged man, even eighty years old. He had provided the king with sustenance while he stayed at Mahanaim; for he was a very great man.
The king said to Barzillai, “Come over with me, and I will sustain you with me in Jerusalem.”
Barzillai said to the king, “How many are the days of the years of my life, that I should go up with the king to Jerusalem?

I am eighty years old, today. Can I discern between good and bad? Can your servant taste what I eat or what I drink? Can I hear the voice of singing men and singing women any more? Why then should your servant be a burden to my lord the king?
Your servant would but just go over the Jordan with the king. Why should the king repay me with such a reward?

Please let your servant turn back again, that I may die in my own city, by the grave of my father and my mother. But behold, your servant Chimham; let him go over with my lord the king; and do to him what shall seem good to you.”
The king answered, “Chimham shall go over with me, and I will do to him that which shall seem good to you. Whatever you request of me, that I will do for you.”
All the people went over the Jordan, and the king went over. Then the king kissed Barzillai, and blessed him; and he returned to his own place.
So the king went over to Gilgal, and Chimham went over with him. All the people of Judah brought the king over, and also half the people of Israel.

Behold, all the men of Israel came to the king, and said to the king, “Why have our brothers the men of Judah stolen you away, and brought the king, and his household, over the Jordan, and all David’s men with him?”

All the men of Judah answered the men of Israel, “Because the king is a close relative to us. Why then are you angry about this matter? Have we eaten at all at the king’s cost? Or has he given us any gift?”

The men of Israel answered the men of Judah, and said, “We have ten parts in the king, and we have also more claim to David than you. Why then did you despise us, that our advice should not be first had in bringing back our king?” The words of the men of Judah were fiercer than the words of the men of Israel.

footnotes.content: The king's sorrow has reached even his commander's ears. How often do our griefs speak louder than our triumphs—and how revealing they are of what we truly love.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A day of victory becomes a day of mourning because the people understand the king's heart. There is a fellowship in grief that bonds a people more truly than any conquest could.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Shame steals people away as surely as defeat does. When a leader grieves instead of celebrating, followers wonder if victory itself has meaning.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A father's cry is the deepest sound a man can make. David's repetition—"my son"—speaks the ache that no single word can contain. We grieve those we love, and love is the truest measure of a life.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Joab speaks hard truth because he sees the moment clearly: a king's despair is draining the faithfulness from those who shed their blood for him. Sometimes love demands we speak when silence would be gentler.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Joab names it plainly—the king's sorrow has reversed his affections. He mourns the son who rose against him while those who loved him faithfully watch in bewilderment. How swiftly grief can twist the visible truth.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Joab's oath carries the weight of command, not mere counsel. There is a season for private grief and a season when a leader must rise and appear before the people, lest his sorrow become their ruin. The Lord calls leaders to lay aside what they feel for the sake of those who depend on them.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The king hears the rebuke and obeys it—he takes his seat in the gate, the place of judgment and rule. His servants, seeing him sit in authority again, begin to return from their scattered tents. A leader's posture teaches his people more than his words do.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The people remember David's first victories as king—how he delivered them from enemies. But his flight from Absalom has unsettled their trust. We often forget a person's whole life in the shadow of one failure or loss.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Here is the pivot: Absalom, whom they anointed to replace David, is dead. The momentum of revolt has broken with him. Now the people argue whether to bring the king home—not from duty alone, but from the doubt that grips them when a way forward suddenly becomes unclear.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: David sends word through the priests to Judah, his own tribe. He does not command them back; he asks why they are last in bringing the king home. He appeals to their kinship and their shame at the hesitation.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "You are my bone and my flesh"—David speaks to Judah as a family member speaks, not as a king to subjects. He reminds them of intimacy, of blood ties. When we are broken by losses, we often need to be reminded that we are still beloved by those nearest us.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: David reaches out to Amasa—Absalom's general, his own kinsman—and names him captain in Joab's place. It is an act of mercy and reconciliation, a way of saying: let us begin again. But it will wound Joab, who sees ingratitude in it.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: David's appeal works—the hearts of the men of Judah turn "as one man." One faithful word, spoken through the right messenger at the right moment, can gather a scattered people and give them one mind again.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The Jordan is more than a river here—it is the line between exile and home. David crosses it at Gilgal, the place where Israel first camped after entering the Promised Land generations before. The crossing marks his return not only to power but to the land itself.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Shimei the Benjamite hastens to meet David. We remember him from 2 Samuel 16, cursing the king as he fled. Now he comes to greet him on his return. People often rush to mend what shame has broken when the moment shifts.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A thousand men of Benjamin come with Shimei, along with Ziba and his household. The show of force and numbers speaks to Shimei's anxiety—he fears for his life and brings witnesses and evidence of his loyalty.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A ferry boat carries the king's household across. Shimei falls before David—a gesture of surrender and supplication. He has come to throw himself on the king's mercy, as one who once cursed now stands powerless to protect himself.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Shimei confesses his sin at the moment of David's return—not before, not after, but now. He speaks of perversity on the day Jerusalem fell, asking David not to remember it. He is asking not just for forgiveness but for amnesia, for grace that erases.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Shimei names himself "the first of all the house of Joseph to go down to meet" the king. This is both confession and claim—he confesses his sin but also claims that his haste to reconcile puts him first among penitents.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Abishai son of Zeruiah speaks for swift justice: Shimei cursed the Lord's anointed and should die for it. The law is clear; the offense real. But Abishai does not see the larger grace beginning to work in David's heart.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: David turns on the sons of Zeruiah—men of war who do not understand that this day is not a day for killing. He asks: shall anyone die today in Israel? He has learned that the victory is not complete until mercy is woven through it.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The king swears to Shimei: "You will not die." This oath mirrors one David made long ago to Jonathan—binding and unconditional. In the eyes of Israel, the king's word is law, and once given, it cannot be unmade.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Mephibosheth comes with neither groomed feet nor trimmed beard—the signs of mourning and want. From the day the king departed until his return in peace, Mephibosheth kept himself unwashed and unkempt. His body tells the story of his faithfulness and grief.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: David's question is pointed: "Why didn't you go with me?" It strikes at the one doubt—was Mephibosheth truly faithful, or did he remain behind to see which way the wind would blow?
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Mephibosheth speaks quickly: his servant Ziba deceived him. He saddled a donkey for Mephibosheth to ride with the king, but because Mephibosheth is lame, he could not mount. His disability becomes his defense—he wanted to go but could not.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Mephibosheth calls David "as an angel of God"—one who sees into the heart and judges truly. He surrenders all defense to David's wisdom, knowing that truth is not easily proven but must be received as a gift from one who loves well.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Mephibosheth speaks from profound gratitude: his whole family were "dead men" before David showed them mercy, yet David set him at his own table. To be received into a king's household is resurrection for one born under a curse of inheritance.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: David cuts short Mephibosheth's self-abasement: divide the land with Ziba. The king will not hear more of the quarrel. Sometimes a leader's justice is swift not because wisdom demands it, but because grace does—to spare a man the agony of protesting his own worth.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Mephibosheth's reply is the measure of his relief: let Ziba take all, because the king has come home in peace. He cares nothing for property; he cares only that the king's return means his own life is secured.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Barzillai the Gileadite comes from Rogelim, the place where David hid during the rebellion. Barzillai sustained David when he was in want; now he comes to conduct the king back across the Jordan. True friends do not abandon in affliction nor vanish when fortune returns.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Barzillai is eighty years old—a very aged man in David's time. At Mahanaim he provided sustenance for the king's household, an act of great kindness and no small cost. His age speaks to the enduring faithfulness of his house to David's rightful rule.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: David honors Barzillai's faithfulness by inviting him to Jerusalem, offering to sustain him in his old age. It is David's way of saying: your kindness will not be forgotten; your latter years will be cared for.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Barzillai asks: how many years are left to me, that I should go up to Jerusalem? He speaks not bitterly but with the clarity that comes at eighty. He knows his time is short and his strength failing.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Barzillai lists his infirmities with plain speech—he cannot taste food or drink, cannot hear music, his senses have dimmed. He asks plainly: why should an old man be a burden to a king he loves? There is dignity in his refusal, not ingratitude.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Barzillai says he would cross the Jordan with David, but why should the king repay such small service with such a reward? He speaks of his journey itself as reward enough—to escort the king home and see him restored is gift sufficient.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Barzillai asks to turn back and die in his own city, near the grave of his father and mother. His last wish is to rest where his roots run deep. He offers his son Chimham instead, trusting David to honor him as he honored the father.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: David honors Barzillai's wish and makes Chimham his ward. He promises to do whatever Barzillai requests, a blank oath that speaks his gratitude more truly than words could. The king binds himself to the faithful servant's house.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The king kisses Barzillai and blesses him—the parting of two men who have walked through fire together. Barzillai returns to his own place, and David to Jerusalem. Their bond is sealed in that moment of embrace and benediction.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: All the people of Judah bring the king over the Jordan, and half the people of Israel as well. Gilgal, where Israel first camped after crossing into the Promised Land, witnesses again the crossing of a king—this time, the people restored to their king and their king restored to them.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: But immediately the men of Israel cry out in protest: "Why have our brothers stolen you away?" The unity is fragile; the question of who truly brought the king home—Judah or Israel—stirs the old rivalry that will soon tear the kingdom apart.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Judah's answer is simple and clear: the king is their kinsman; they have taken nothing from Israel, no gain has passed between them. But the words sound defensive, and Judah's haste to answer shows the sting of the accusation.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Israel's reply comes fiercer still—they claim ten parts in the king and more right to David than Judah does. Their grievance is not petty; it carries the weight of the old division. Readers today hear an echo of the fracture that ended David's united kingdom within a generation—the same pride and rivalry that opened the door to civil war.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
